column2: Things turned out as Wemmick had predicted. I soon had a chance to compare my guardian’s household with that of his cashier and clerk. When I came into the office from Walworth, my guardian was in his room washing his hands with scented soap. He called me over and gave me the invitation for myself and my friends that Wemmick had told me to expect. “No ceremony,” he stipulated. “No dinner dress, and let’s say tomorrow.” I asked where we were to come, for I had no idea where he lived. I believe it was his general objection to making anything like an admission that prompted his reply: “Come here, and I’ll take you home with me.” I’ll take this opportunity to remark that he washed his clients off him as if he were a surgeon or a dentist. He had a little closet fitted out for the purpose in his room. The scented soap made it smell like a perfumer’s shop. An unusually large roller towel hung inside the door. Whenever he came in from a police court or saw a client out, he washed his hands and wiped and dried them all over that towel. When my friends and I called at six the next day, he seemed to have had a case of a darker complexion than usual, for we found him with his head stuck into the closet, not only washing his hands but bathing his face and gargling his throat. Even when he had done all that and gone all the way round the towel, he got his penknife out and scraped the case from under his nails before putting on his coat.

He took us to a house on the south side of Gerrard Street in Soho. It was rather stately in its way, though sadly in need of paint, with dirty windows. He took out his key and let us into a bare, gloomy stone hall that saw little use. Then up a dark brown staircase we went, into a row of three dark brown rooms on the first floor. There were carved garlands on the panelled walls, and as he stood among them welcoming us, I know what kind of loops I thought they looked like.

Dinner was laid in the best of the rooms. The second was his dressing room, the third his bedroom. He told us he had the whole house but rarely used more of it than we now saw. The table looked comfortable — no silver, of course — and beside his chair stood a roomy serving stand with an assortment of bottles and decanters and four dishes of fruit for dessert. I noticed throughout the meal that he kept everything within reach and handed it all out himself.

The room held a bookcase. The spines gave me some idea of its contents: evidence, criminal law, lives of criminals, trials, acts of Parliament and the like. Like his watch chain, the furniture was solid and good. Still, it had an official look, and there was nothing in sight that was there merely for decoration. In a corner stood a little table of papers with a shaded lamp. In that respect too he seemed to bring the office home, ready to wheel it out of an evening and get to work.

I supposed her to be about forty, though I may have thought her younger than she was. She was rather tall, lithe and quick, extremely pale, with large faded eyes and a mass of flowing hair. I can’t say whether some disorder of the heart made her lips part as if she were out of breath and gave her face that strange look of sudden alarm and flutter. But I know I’d been to see Macbeth at the theatre a night or two before, and her face seemed to shift in a current of fiery air like the faces I had seen rise out of the witches’ cauldron.

She set the dish down, touched my guardian lightly on the arm to let him know dinner was ready, and vanished. We sat down at the round table. My guardian kept Drummle on one side of him, with Startop on the other. The housekeeper had brought in a splendid dish of fish. An equally choice joint of mutton followed, then an equally choice bird. Our host handed out sauces, wines, whatever else we wanted, all of the best, from his serving stand. Once they’d gone round the table he always put them back. In the same way he dealt out clean plates and knives and forks for each course and dropped the used ones into two baskets on the floor beside him. No servant but the housekeeper appeared. She brought in every dish, and each time I saw a face rising out of the cauldron. Years later I made a dreadful likeness of the woman by having someone pass behind a bowl of flaming spirits in a dark room. Apart from the flowing hair, the two faces had nothing in common.

Between the housekeeper’s striking appearance and what Wemmick had told me, I paid particular attention to her. Whenever she was in the room she watched my guardian closely. When she set a dish before him she seemed reluctant to take her hands away, as if she dreaded being called back and wanted him to speak while she was still close by, if he had anything to say. I thought I could see in his manner that he knew this and meant to keep her in suspense.

Dinner passed cheerfully. My guardian seemed to follow our lead in the conversation, but I knew he was wrenching the weakest points of our characters out of us. In my own case, my taste for extravagance, for patronising Herbert and for boasting of my great prospects had all come out before I quite realised I had opened my mouth. It was the same with all of us, but especially with Drummle. My guardian had screwed his tendency to make grudging, suspicious digs at the rest of us out of him before the fish was cleared away.

It was later, when we got to the cheese, that we began to talk about our rowing feats and tease Drummle about his habit of coming up behind us at night in that slow, amphibious way of his. Drummle told our host he greatly preferred our absence to our company, that he was more than a match for us in skill, and that in strength he could scatter us like chaff. Somehow, without our seeing how, my guardian got him worked up almost to ferocity over this trifle. He bared his arm and put his hand round it to show us the muscle. Then we all sat there baring and measuring our arms like so many fools.

He took his hand off hers and turned the wrist palm up on the table. She brought out the other hand from behind her back and held the two side by side. This second wrist was badly disfigured, with deep scars crossing and recrossing it. As she held her hands out she took her eyes off Mr. Jaggers and looked watchfully at each of us in turn.
“At half past nine, gentlemen,” he said, “we must break up. Please make the most of your time. I’m glad to see you all. Mr. Drummle, I drink to you.”

If he meant to bring Drummle out still further by singling him out, he succeeded perfectly. In sulky triumph Drummle treated the rest of us with increasingly offensive contempt until he was quite unbearable. Through every stage Mr. Jaggers watched him with the same strange interest. Drummle actually seemed to give the wine an extra relish for Mr. Jaggers.

At this point Startop took him in hand, with much better grace than I had shown, and urged him to be a little more agreeable. Startop was a bright, lively young fellow and Drummle his exact opposite, so that Drummle always tended to regard him as a personal affront. He made a coarse, clumsy retort, and Startop tried to turn the talk aside with a little joke that made us all laugh. Drummle resented this small success more than anything. Without threat or warning he pulled his hands from his pockets, dropped his round shoulders, swore and snatched up a large glass. He would have thrown it at his opponent’s head if our host hadn’t deftly caught it the instant he raised it.

The front door hadn’t yet closed, so I thought I would leave Herbert there a moment and run back upstairs for a word with my guardian. I found him in his dressing room among his collection of boots, already hard at work washing his hands of us.
About a month later the Spider’s time with Mr. Pocket was up for good. To the great relief of everyone in the house except Mrs. Pocket, he went home to the family hole.

As usual, there were people lurking about when we stepped into the street, plainly anxious to speak to him. But there was something so final about the halo of scented soap round his person that they gave it up for the day. As we walked west, now and then a face in the crowd recognised him. Whenever that happened, he spoke louder to me. Apart from that he never showed the slightest sign that he knew anyone or noticed anyone knew him.

The housekeeper was clearing the table. My guardian took no notice of her. He leaned back in his chair with his face turned half away from her, biting the side of his forefinger and showing an interest in Drummle that baffled me. As she stretched her hand across the table, he suddenly clapped his great hand over it like a trap. He did it so suddenly and so smartly that we all stopped in the middle of our foolish contest.

As he spoke in that leisurely, appraising way, she went on looking at each of us in turn as we sat round the table. The moment he stopped, her eyes went back to him. “That’ll do, Molly,” Mr. Jaggers said with a slight nod. “You’ve been admired and you can go.” She withdrew her hands and left the room. Mr. Jaggers put the decanters on the table from his serving stand, filled his glass and passed the wine round.

At this hint we all got up to leave. Before we reached the front door, Startop was cheerfully calling Drummle “old boy” as if nothing had happened. But the old boy was so far from responding that he wouldn’t even walk to Hammersmith on the same side of the street. Herbert and I, who were staying in town, watched them go off on opposite sides, Startop ahead and Drummle lagging in the shadow of the houses, much as he used to follow in his boat.
